title: Nonlinear Feedback in Josephson Circuit Optimization: Application to a Kerr-Reversal JTWPA
authors: Emanuele Palumbo, Alessandro Alocco, Andrea Celotto, Luca Fasolo, Bernardo Galvano, Patrizia Livreri, Emanuele Enrico
abstract: Optimizing Josephson-based nonlinear microwave devices is computationally demanding because the straightforward approach requires exploring broad circuit parameter spaces through expensive nonlinear simulations. Josephson Circuits Optimizer addresses this problem by using harmonic balance simulations in two stages: fast linear simulations to select promising circuit configurations according to properties such as impedance and phase matching, followed by nonlinear simulations to optimize their operating conditions. However, pump-induced effects such as impedance renormalization and Kerr-induced modifications of phase matching are not captured during the initial linear stage. We therefore introduce a nonlinear feedback extension that transfers information from the pumped response back to the linear optimization. The approach is investigated using a Josephson traveling-wave parametric amplifier with a reversed-Kerr architecture, whose model is validated against experimental gain measurements. We then evaluate the difference between the linear and pumped response values of a metric based on the input reflection coefficient, while excluding configurations with insufficient third-harmonic suppression. This discrepancy is considered a candidate feedback observable, as it exhibits features similar to the gain landscape, supporting its use in subsequent optimization cycles.
summary: This paper addresses the computational bottleneck in optimizing nonlinear Josephson microwave circuits by proposing a nonlinear feedback extension to the standard optimization workflow. The method uses the difference between linear and pumped simulation results as a diagnostic observable to guide subsequent, more accurate optimization cycles. This allows for the efficient design of high-performance parametric amplifiers by incorporating complex nonlinear physics into the initial design phase.
main_problem: Optimizing Josephson-based nonlinear microwave devices is computationally expensive because standard methods fail to account for pump-induced nonlinear effects during initial linear parameter sweeps.
main_result: The authors introduce a nonlinear feedback mechanism using the discrepancy between linear and pumped response metrics, showing this observable contains crucial information about amplifier performance missed by linear optimization.
method: They developed a two-stage optimization framework, extending the initial linear search with an iterative feedback loop that incorporates nonlinear simulation results back into the linear metric update.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a Josephson Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifier (JTWPA) utilizing a reversed-Kerr architecture. The model is implemented using a lumped-element circuit description.
key_observables: Input reflection coefficient ($S_{11}$) in the signal band, third-harmonic suppression ($S_{11,dB}(3f_p)$), and the discrepancy ($\Delta M$) between linear and pumped metric values.
important_parameters: Circuit parameters like inductive bias ($I_0$) and ground capacitance ($C_g$), and operating frequencies (5–9 GHz signal band).
main_assumptions: The initial linear optimization ignores nonlinear effects like impedance renormalization and Kerr-induced dispersion modifications; the feedback observable must mimic the gain landscape features.
figures_summary: Figure 3 validates the model by comparing simulated and measured signal gain. Figure 4 compares the linear metric, nonlinear metric, discrepancy ($\Delta M$), and average gain across the parameter space, highlighting the difference between linear and maximum-gain configurations.
paper_structure: The paper outlines the limitations of the standard two-stage optimization (JCO), introduces the nonlinear feedback extension, validates the model against experimental gain measurements, and finally demonstrates the use of the discrepancy ($\Delta M$) as the candidate feedback observable for iterative optimization.
why_interesting: This work bridges advanced circuit simulation techniques with quantum optics/AMO concepts by treating the optimization of nonlinear quantum devices (like parametric amplifiers) as an iterative, feedback-controlled process, which has parallels in quantum control theory.
